questions.stem: Common SALT — sodium chloride — has the chemical formula:
questions.explanation: SODIUM CHLORIDE (NaCl) — common table salt. Ionic compound. Essential for animal life (Na+ and Cl- ions key for nerve/muscle function, osmotic balance). COMMON NAMES to FORMULAS: (1) Table salt = NaCl; (2) BAKING SODA = SODIUM BICARBONATE = NaHCO₃; (3) WASHING SODA = SODIUM CARBONATE = Na₂CO₃ (decahydrate Na₂CO₃·10H₂O); (4) CAUSTIC SODA = SODIUM HYDROXIDE = NaOH; (5) BLEACHING POWDER = CALCIUM OXYCHLORIDE = Ca(OCl)₂ / CaOCl₂; (6) QUICKLIME = CALCIUM OXIDE = CaO; (7) SLAKED LIME = CALCIUM HYDROXIDE = Ca(OH)₂; (8) LIMESTONE / MARBLE / CHALK = CALCIUM CARBONATE = CaCO₃; (9) PLASTER OF PARIS = CALCIUM SULPHATE HEMIHYDRATE = CaSO₄·½H₂O; (10) GYPSUM = CALCIUM SULPHATE DIHYDRATE = CaSO₄·2H₂O; (11) VINEGAR = dilute acetic acid = CH₃COOH; (12) EPSOM SALT = MgSO₄·7H₂O; (13) BLUE VITRIOL / COPPER SULPHATE = CuSO₄·5H₂O (blue crystals); (14) GREEN VITRIOL = FeSO₄·7H₂O; (15) WHITE VITRIOL = ZnSO₄·7H₂O; (16) MILK OF MAGNESIA = Mg(OH)₂ (antacid).

questions.stem: SOAP and DETERGENTS both clean, but differ in:

options.option_text: Chemical nature: SOAP is sodium/potassium salt of long-chain fatty acids; DETERGENT is a synthetic salt of sulphonic acid (alkylbenzenesulphonates)

questions.explanation: SOAPS vs DETERGENTS: SOAPS = sodium (or potassium) salts of long-chain FATTY ACIDS (e.g., sodium stearate, palmitate, oleate). Made by SAPONIFICATION — fat/oil + NaOH → soap + glycerol. POTASSIUM soaps are softer (shaving creams). Sodium soaps are harder (bar soaps). PROBLEMS with soap: forms INSOLUBLE 'SCUM' with hard water (Ca²+/Mg²+ ions) → wastes soap + doesn't clean well. DETERGENTS = SYNTHETIC surfactants, typically sodium salts of SULPHONIC acids (alkylbenzene sulphonates — ABS/LAS). ADVANTAGES: work in hard water (Ca/Mg sulphonate salts are soluble), cold water, more lathering. Both have HYDROPHOBIC TAIL (long hydrocarbon chain — dissolves in grease) + HYDROPHILIC HEAD (-COO⁻ or -SO₃⁻ — dissolves in water) → form MICELLES that trap dirt/grease and wash it away. Early detergents had BRANCHED chains (non-biodegradable, polluted water); modern detergents are LINEAR (LAS — biodegradable). First synthetic detergent: BASF Germany 1907. Persil 1907, commercial household products by 1950s in India (Surf 1959 by Hindustan Lever).

questions.stem: The chemical used to DISINFECT DRINKING WATER + KILL BACTERIA in municipal water supplies is:
questions.explanation: CHLORINATION — adding chlorine gas (Cl₂) or chlorine compounds (bleaching powder = CaOCl₂, calcium hypochlorite, sodium hypochlorite NaOCl) to drinking water to kill pathogens. Chlorine reacts with water to form hypochlorous acid (HOCl) which is a powerful oxidiser. DOSE: ~0.2-1 mg/L residual chlorine. Introduced in the West around 1900s; in India early 20th c. + mass implementation post-1950s — eliminated waterborne epidemics (cholera, typhoid). Drawback: can form TRIHALOMETHANES (THMs) — potential carcinogens at high levels. ALTERNATIVES: OZONE (O₃ — powerful, no aftertaste, but no residual protection); UV LIGHT (kills microbes, no chemicals); IODINE tablets (backpacking); BOILING; FILTRATION (activated carbon, RO). OTHER chemical uses in daily life: BLEACH — sodium hypochlorite (NaOCl) for laundry + cleaning, calcium hypochlorite for pools. ANTACIDS — magnesium hydroxide (milk of magnesia), aluminium hydroxide, calcium carbonate; neutralise stomach acid. FIRE EXTINGUISHERS — CO₂, foam, powder. BAKING POWDER — NaHCO₃ + acid (cream of tartar) + starch — releases CO₂ to raise dough. VINEGAR — 5-8% acetic acid.

questions.stem: Which gas is used to RIPEN green fruits artificially (e.g. green bananas turning yellow)?
questions.explanation: ETHYLENE (C₂H₄) — a natural PLANT HORMONE that triggers FRUIT RIPENING. Released naturally by fruits as they ripen ('climacteric' fruits — banana, apple, mango, tomato, avocado, pear). Used commercially to trigger uniform ripening: (a) ETHYLENE GAS in sealed chambers — safe, preferred method. (b) CALCIUM CARBIDE (CaC₂) — BANNED in India for fruit ripening since 2011 (Prevention of Food Adulteration Act 1954, Section 44-AA). Calcium carbide reacts with moisture to release ACETYLENE + also contains traces of ARSENIC + PHOSPHORUS — toxic. Common in India despite ban. Also unsafe: burning newspaper / kerosene fumes in closed banana warehouses. Another ripening agent: ETHEPHON (2-chloroethylphosphonic acid — releases ethylene slowly; used as a plant growth regulator). OTHER HORMONES: (1) AUXINS (growth, root development — IAA indole acetic acid); (2) GIBBERELLINS (stem elongation, seed germination); (3) CYTOKININS (cell division); (4) ABSCISIC ACID (stress response, bud dormancy); (5) ETHYLENE (fruit ripening + flower senescence).

options.option_text: Calcium carbonate (CaCO₃ in the form of aragonite) + conchiolin (organic matrix)

questions.explanation: PEARLS = predominantly CALCIUM CARBONATE (CaCO₃) in the form of ARAGONITE crystals (a specific crystal form of CaCO₃), held together by CONCHIOLIN (a protein). Same material as MOTHER-OF-PEARL (nacre) that lines the inside of oyster shells. Formation: when an irritant (sand grain, parasite) gets into an OYSTER or mussel, the animal secretes concentric layers of nacre around it → pearl. NATURAL pearls are rare; 99% of jewelry pearls today are CULTURED (a tiny bead is inserted into the oyster, which then coats it). Pearl qualities: size, shape (round best), lustre, surface, colour (white/pink/black/gold depending on oyster species + water conditions). India's Southern pearl fisheries: Gulf of Mannar (TN), earlier Gulf of Kutch. Famous pearls: LA PEREGRINA (Elizabeth Taylor), PEARL OF LAO TZU (largest ~6.4 kg), TAJ MAHAL PEARL. OTHER 'GEMS/STONES' by chemistry: DIAMOND = pure CARBON in tetrahedral lattice; RUBY + SAPPHIRE = aluminium oxide (Al₂O₃) with Cr/Fe/Ti impurities; EMERALD = beryllium aluminium silicate (Be₃Al₂Si₆O₁₈); QUARTZ = SiO₂; TURQUOISE = hydrated copper aluminium phosphate; MARBLE = metamorphosed CaCO₃; GRANITE = igneous rock (quartz + feldspar + mica); CORAL = CaCO₃ with organic matter.

questions.stem: Which chemical is called the 'KING OF CHEMICALS' due to its industrial importance?
questions.explanation: SULPHURIC ACID (H₂SO₄) — called the 'KING OF CHEMICALS' because of its vast industrial usage. World production: ~300 million tonnes/year (> any other manufactured chemical). INDUSTRIAL USES: (1) FERTILISER production (super-phosphate, ammonium sulphate — ~50% of global H₂SO₄ goes here); (2) Lead-acid BATTERIES (car batteries use dilute H₂SO₄ as electrolyte); (3) Petroleum refining (catalyst, cleaning); (4) Detergent manufacture (sulphonation); (5) Dye + pigment industry; (6) Steel pickling (to remove oxide layers); (7) Lab uses (as a drying agent — hygroscopic + oxidising); (8) Chemical synthesis. Industrial production: CONTACT PROCESS (S → SO₂ → SO₃ → H₂SO₄) using V₂O₅ catalyst. Discovered by alchemist Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721-815 AD) + Muhammad ibn Zakariya al-Razi (c. 865-925). Historical name: 'OIL OF VITRIOL' (thick oil-like appearance). Very corrosive — causes severe burns. India is the 5th-largest producer globally. OTHER IMPORTANT INDUSTRIAL CHEMICALS: AMMONIA (NH₃, Haber-Bosch process, for fertilisers + explosives), CHLORINE (Cl₂, chlor-alkali process, for PVC + disinfection), ETHYLENE (basis of polyethylene, PVC, ethanol), METHANOL (fuel, formaldehyde production).

questions.stem: 'STAINLESS STEEL' is resistant to corrosion because of a thin protective layer of which oxide on its surface?

options.option_text: Chromium(III) oxide (Cr₂O₃) — forms a passive self-healing layer

questions.explanation: STAINLESS STEEL corrosion resistance: due to a thin (<10 nm), invisible, impermeable layer of CHROMIUM(III) OXIDE (Cr₂O₃) that forms spontaneously on the surface. It's PASSIVE + SELF-HEALING — if scratched, re-forms immediately in the presence of oxygen. Hence 'stainless' / 'rustless'. Minimum chromium content for stainless steel: 10.5% (by weight). Invented 1913 by HARRY BREARLEY (Sheffield, UK). GRADES of stainless steel: (1) 18/8 or 304 — 18% Cr + 8% Ni — most common (kitchenware, utensils); (2) 316 — adds 2-3% Mo — better corrosion resistance (marine, chemical plants, surgical); (3) 410, 420, 440 — martensitic, heat-treatable — knives, cutlery. Rust on normal iron: Fe → Fe₂O₃·xH₂O (red-brown, flaky, NOT protective — falls off, exposing fresh iron). Corrosion rate depends on Cr content + environment. Other passivating oxides: ALUMINIUM → Al₂O₃ layer (why aluminium looks dull grey, not shiny); TITANIUM → TiO₂; COPPER → Cu₂O (reddish patina → green basic carbonate 'verdigris' over time — Statue of Liberty is copper patinated green). HOT DIP GALVANISATION (Zn coating on iron) — Zn preferentially corrodes, protecting iron even if scratched (SACRIFICIAL protection).
